questions.q: The Bene Israel are a Jewish community of India. Where did they live?
o: On the Konkan coast, just south of Mumbai
On the Malabar coast, in present-day Kerala
At Sanjan, on the coast of Gujarat
In George Town, in present-day Chennai
questions.a: On the Konkan coast, just south of Mumbai, after their ship was wrecked in a storm near that coast.

questions.q: What is a synagogue?
o: A place of worship for Jews, where services and ceremonies like weddings are held
A temple where the Parsis keep their sacred fire burning
The holy book of the Jews, also called the Torah
A house of worship of the Baha'is, such as the Lotus Temple
questions.a: A synagogue is a place of worship for Jews where religious services and special ceremonies like weddings are held.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Jews in India.
I. The Bene Israel grew to become the largest Jewish community in India, numbering over 25,000 shortly after India gained independence.
II. The Raja of Kochi gave the Jews land for a fixed number of years and charged them rent for it.
III. The Jews who settled near Cochin arrived long after the Bene Israel.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the Raja of Kochi granted them land free of cost 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'. Statement III is right: the Bene Israel came around 175 BCE (according to some scholars), while the groups near Cochin came between the 12th and 19th centuries.

questions.q: (a) At which event, in which city and year, did Swami Vivekananda say he was proud to belong to a nation that had sheltered the persecuted? (b) Name the two peoples whose remnants, he said, India had sheltered.
questions.a: (a) At the World Parliament of Religions held at Chicago in 1893. (b) The Israelites (Jews) and the Zoroastrians.
s: (a) World Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893
(b) The Israelites (Jews) and the Zoroastrians

questions.q: Your class is preparing a fact file on 'Jews in India' for the school notice board. Write one line under each heading: (a) who the Jews are, as the chapter defines them; (b) how the Bene Israel came to settle in India; (c) what the Raja of Kochi gave the Jews who settled near Cochin; (d) what those Jews built, and what it allowed them to do.
questions.a: (a) Members of the people and cultural community originating from the ancient Hebrews of Israel, traditionally linked to the religion of Judaism. (b) Their ship was caught in a storm and wrecked near the Konkan coast; the survivors settled and started a new life. (c) Land free of cost 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'. (d) A synagogue, which let them practise their faith even as they became part of Indian society.
s: (a) People and cultural community from the ancient Hebrews of Israel, linked to Judaism
(b) Shipwrecked in a storm near the Konkan coast; survivors settled and began a new life
(c) Land free of cost 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'
(d) A synagogue, letting them practise their faith while becoming part of Indian society

questions.q: True or False: A survey form asks only one question, 'Do you follow the religion of Judaism?' Ruth says, 'Going by the chapter's note on Jews, this one question will find every person who may be identified as Jewish.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter's note says a Jew may be identified either by descent from Jewish ancestry or through conversion, and that Jewish identity may be defined on the basis of religion, culture, history or ethnicity. A person of Jewish descent or culture who does not follow the religion would be missed by a question about religion alone.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: identity may rest on descent, culture, history or ethnicity, not religion alone, so some people would be missed

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The Jews who settled near Cochin came only to trade, bought their land from the Raja, and had to hide their religion.' Test each of his three points against the chapter.
questions.a: His claim is wrong on all three points. (1) They arrived between the 12th and 19th centuries because they faced persecution in their own countries, not simply for trade. (2) The Raja of Kochi granted them land free of cost, 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'; they did not buy it. (3) They built a synagogue and practised their faith openly even as they became part of Indian society.
s: Reason for coming: they fled persecution in their own countries
Land was granted free of cost by the Raja, not bought
They built a synagogue and practised their faith openly

questions.q: A project board reads: 'The Bene Israel: a few survivors of a shipwreck near the Konkan coast, around 175 BCE.' The teacher asks the student to add how the story continued. (a) What had the community grown into shortly after India gained independence? Give the chapter's figure. (b) Explain what this growth suggests about the community's life in India over the centuries.
questions.a: (a) It had become the largest Jewish community in India, numbering over 25,000. (b) A handful of survivors could grow into the largest Jewish community only if they lived and settled securely in India for many generations and kept their identity as a Jewish community, as the chapter says they started a new life here.
s: (a) Largest Jewish community in India, over 25,000
(b) Growth shows secure settlement over generations while staying a Jewish community

questions.q: Kavya reads that the Bene Israel lost their holy books when their ship was wrecked near the Konkan coast, yet they still remembered their prayer, which says there is only one God. What does this detail best show about them?
o: They held on to the central belief of their faith even without its written texts
They had stopped following their faith by the time they reached India
They learnt the belief in one God from the people of the Konkan coast
They lost their faith with their books and found it again among the Jews of Kochi
questions.a: They held on to the central belief of their faith, that there is only one God, even after losing their holy books.

questions.q:
At a school assembly in Thane, Neel reads out Swami Vivekananda's words from Chicago in 1893: 'I am proud to belong to a nation which has sheltered the persecuted and the refugees of all religions and all nations of the Earth.' He adds that the speaker was also proud of a religion that was 'still fostering the remnant of the grand Zoroastrian nation'. His friend Asha says, 'So in 1893 he was talking about every community in our chapter, including the Polish children and the Tibetans.'
(a) Which community in the chapter follows the Zoroastrian faith, and where in India does its ancient sacred fire still burn?
(b) Between which years were the Polish orphans saved, and in which year was the Dalai Lama granted asylum in India?
(c) Evaluate Asha's statement using the dates.
(d) Name one other community from the chapter whose shelter in India had begun long before 1893, giving the date or period the chapter gives for it.
questions.a: (a) The Parsis; the sacred fire burns in Udvada, a short distance from where they first arrived. (b) The orphans were saved between 1942 and 1946; the Dalai Lama was granted asylum in 1959. (c) Asha is wrong: both events came decades after 1893 (1942 is 49 years later and 1959 is 66 years later), so Vivekananda could not have been speaking of them; they only show that India went on doing what he described. (d) Any one: the Bene Israel (around 175 BCE, according to some scholars); the Jews near Cochin (between the 12th and 19th centuries); the Syriac Christians (whose troubles began from the 4th century CE).
s: (a) The Parsis; Udvada
(c) Rejects Asha's claim: both events came after 1893, so he could not mean them
(d) One earlier community with its chapter date or period

questions.q: Zoroastrianism, the faith of the Parsis, is one of the world's oldest religions. Who founded it?
o: The prophet Zarathushtra, in Central Asia
The Raja of Kochi, on the Malabar coast
questions.a: The prophet Zarathushtra founded Zoroastrianism in Central Asia; it is based on the worship of one God, Ahura Mazda.

questions.q:
Match each word in Column I with its meaning in Column II, as the chapter uses it.
Column I: 1. Ahura Mazda  2. Avesta  3. Udvada  4. Sanjan
Column II: P. The Parsis' ancient sacred text  Q. The one God worshipped in Zoroastrianism  R. The coastal kingdom of Raja Jadi Rana  S. The place where the ancient sacred fire still burns
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Ahura Mazda is the one God of Zoroastrianism; the Avesta is the Parsis' ancient sacred text; the sacred fire still burns at Udvada; Sanjan was Raja Jadi Rana's kingdom in coastal Gujarat.

questions.q: (a) Which ancient language did the Syriac Christians use in their worship and traditions? (b) On which coast of India did they arrive, and which present-day state is it in?
questions.a: (a) The ancient Syriac language. (b) The Malabar coast, in present-day Kerala.
s: (a) Syriac
(b) Malabar coast, present-day Kerala

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Of which empire was Zoroastrianism the state religion, and for which centuries did that empire last? (b) To whom did that empire fall, and when? (c) State two ways in which Zoroastrians were persecuted after that fall.
questions.a: (a) The Sassanid Empire, from the 3rd to the 7th centuries. (b) To Arab Muslim forces, in the middle of the 7th century. (c) Any two of: forced conversions to Islam; a religious tax (jizya); destruction of their sacred fire temples; social and legal marginalisation.
s: (a) The Sassanid Empire, 3rd to 7th centuries
(b) Fell to Arab Muslim forces in the mid-7th century
(c) Any two forms: forced conversion, jizya, destroyed fire temples, marginalisation

questions.q: Complete a five-line fact card titled 'The Parsis come to India'. Write one line for each heading. (a) The land they left, with its modern name. (b) The sea they sailed across. (c) The region of India they reached, and between which centuries. (d) The one precious thing they carried with them. (e) The country that today has the largest population of followers of Zoroastrianism.
questions.a: (a) Persia, modern-day Iran. (b) The Arabian Sea. (c) India's western coast, in present-day Gujarat, between the 8th and 10th centuries. (d) Their sacred fire. (e) India.
s: (a) Persia (modern-day Iran)
(b) The Arabian Sea
(c) Western coast, present-day Gujarat, 8th to 10th centuries
(d) Their sacred fire
(e) India

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Syriac Christians faced difficulties in the Roman Empire and in the Persian Empire for the same reason.
Reason (R): In the Persian Empire, they were suspected of secretly helping the Romans, who were enemies of Persia.
questions.a: A is false and R is true. The reasons differed: under the Romans they were treated as heretics because some of their beliefs about Christ differed from the official Church, while in Persia they were suspected of secretly helping the Romans.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: True or False: The Parsis sailed to India with a great deal of property, so they could settle in Sanjan without asking its Raja for anything. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Parsis carried little with them, only their sacred fire and some hope of making a home in a place they had heard was safe, and they approached Raja Jadi Rana of Sanjan for a safe place to stay.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: they carried little (their sacred fire and some hope) and approached Raja Jadi Rana for a safe place

questions.q: A heritage booklet from Kerala says: 'The Syriac Christians of India form one single church with no divisions, and they are never called by any other name.' Which correction is supported by the chapter?
o: They are also called 'Syrian Christians' and are divided into several sects.
They are called 'Mappilas' and all belong to a single church.
They are called 'Bene Israel' and are divided into several sects.
They are also called 'Syrian Christians', but they gave up the Syriac language on reaching India.
questions.a: In India the Syriac Christians are also called 'Syrian Christians', and they are divided into several sects.

questions.q:
A museum in Kochi is planning a gallery called 'They Came to the Kerala Coast'. Panel 1: Christians who used the ancient Syriac language in their worship; from the 4th century CE they faced difficulties in West Asia; some travelled eastward along trade routes and reached the Malabar coast. Panel 2: Arab merchants who came to India from the 7th century onward, traded spices and other goods, married local women and helped build the Cheraman Juma Masjid. The curator's draft caption reads: 'Both communities came to Kerala to trade.'
(a) Why were the Syriac Christians sometimes treated as heretics under the Roman Empire?
(b) Which Kerala community did the Arab settlers become part of?
(c) How many centuries separate the starting points given on the two panels? Show your working.
(d) Evaluate the curator's caption and rewrite it as one correct sentence.
questions.a: (a) Because some of their beliefs about Christ were different from those of the official Church. (b) The Mappila Muslim community. (c) 7th century minus 4th century = 3 centuries; the Syriac Christians' troubles began about three centuries before the Arab merchants began coming. (d) The caption is only half right. The Arab merchants came as peaceful traders, but the Syriac Christians came to escape persecution and to live and worship freely; the trade routes were only the path they travelled. A correct caption: 'The Syriac Christians came along trade routes to escape persecution, while the Arab merchants came to trade.'
s: (a) Some of their beliefs about Christ differed from those of the official Church
(b) The Mappila Muslim community
(c) 7 - 4 = 3 centuries
(d) Caption fits the Arabs only; Syriac Christians fled persecution, trade routes were the path; correct rewrite

questions.q: Kiran says, 'To be accepted in India, the Parsis had to give up their own faith and blend in completely.' Evaluate his claim. Use five separate pieces of evidence from the chapter about how the Parsis settled and lived in India, each in one line, and end with your verdict.
questions.a: The claim is wrong on both counts. (1) In the legend, Raja Jadi Rana gave them a secure place after the wise man dissolved sugar in the full jug of milk without spilling it: the legend shows they were accepted to mix in without displacing anyone; it says nothing of their having to give up their faith. (2) They carried their sacred fire with them, and the ancient sacred fire still burns at Udvada, close to where they first arrived. (3) Today India has the largest population of followers of Zoroastrianism in the world, so the faith survived and continued here. (4) They combined their ancient traditions with those of the local culture, so they did blend in, but by combining rather than giving up. (5) Raja Ravi Varma's painting of a Parsi bride getting ready for her wedding shows many aspects of Indian culture, and the Parsis continue to live in India and enrich various aspects of its society. Verdict: the Parsis kept their faith and also became part of Indian life; they did not have to give up one for the other.
s: Legend: secure place given by Raja Jadi Rana; accepted to mix in without displacing anyone
Sacred fire still burns at Udvada
India has the world's largest Zoroastrian population
Combined their traditions with local culture
Ravi Varma painting / Parsis enrich Indian society, and a clear verdict rejecting the claim

questions.q: Which mosque does the chapter call India's oldest mosque, built with the help of early Arab settlers in Kerala?
o: The mosque in George Town, Chennai
questions.a: The Cheraman Juma Masjid in Kerala, which Arab settlers who became part of the Mappila Muslim community helped to build.

questions.q: Where is Armenia, the homeland of the Armenians who settled in India, located?
o: Between Turkey and Azerbaijan, just north of Iran
Between Iran and India, just south of Tibet
On the east coast of Africa, south of Arabia
Between Poland and Turkey, just west of Iran
questions.a: Armenia is a relatively small, mountainous country between Turkey and Azerbaijan, just north of Iran.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Siddis.
I. Over time they have adapted their language to regional influences.
II. They have integrated African religious practices with adopted faiths of Hinduism, Islam or Christianity.
III. They came to India as merchants who traded in spices.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: the Siddis did not come as merchants; they were brought to India as slaves of Arab, Portuguese and British traders.

questions.q: (a) Name three places on India's west coast where many Arab merchants settled. (b) What did they trade?
questions.a: (a) Kerala, Gujarat and Karnataka. (b) Spices and other goods.
s: (a) Kerala, Gujarat and Karnataka
(b) Spices and other goods

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) From which century did Arab merchants come to India? (b) Name two things they did after settling, besides trading. (c) The chapter says they came 'as peaceful traders, not as conquerors'. What does this mean?
questions.a: (a) From the 7th century onward. (b) Any two: married local women; formed new communities (such as the Mappila Muslims in Kerala); helped build the Cheraman Juma Masjid; brought new ideas, culture and religion. (c) They came to do business and live among the people, not to fight and take over the land.
s: (a) From the 7th century
(b) Any two: married local women, formed new communities, helped build the mosque, brought new ideas
(c) Came to trade and live here, not to fight and rule

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Armenians are still remembered in Chennai, though their population there has dwindled to a handful of families.
Reason (R): Armenian Street in George Town memorialises their presence, and St. Mary's Armenian Church stands as a symbol of their faith.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, and R explains A: the street named after them and the mid-18th-century church keep the memory of the Armenians alive in Chennai even though few families remain.

questions.q:
Match each person in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Abdul Hai  2. Lady Juliana  3. Hirabai Lobi  4. Akbar
Column II: P. Doctor in the Mughal royal palace  Q. Chief Justice in Akbar's court  R. Allowed the Armenians to build a church in Agra  S. Siddi woman from Gujarat awarded the Padma Shri
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Abdul Hai was Chief Justice in Akbar's court; Lady Juliana was a doctor in the royal palace; Hirabai Lobi is the Siddi woman from Gujarat awarded the Padma Shri; Akbar allowed the Armenians to build a church in Agra.

questions.q: Armenian merchants settled in Madras around the mid-17th century, and St. Mary's Armenian Church there was built in the mid-18th century. (a) About how many years after settling did they build the church? Show your working. (b) A tour guide says, 'The Armenians were only passing traders in Madras.' Use your answer to (a) and one more fact from the chapter to correct him.
questions.a: (a) Mid-18th century minus mid-17th century is about one century, roughly 1750 - 1650 = 100 years. (b) They were not passing traders: they were still there about a hundred years after arriving and built a church as a symbol of their faith, and the chapter says they became influential in commerce and left a lasting mark on the city's economic and cultural history.
s: (a) About 100 years (mid-17th to mid-18th century)
(b) Stayed a century and built a church; became influential and left a lasting mark, so not passing traders

questions.q: A Class 7 group is making a wall timeline of five events from this section. P: Armenians settle in Madras, drawn by its trade routes. Q: Arab merchants begin coming to India. R: Some Siddis gain prominence in Muslim rulers' armies and briefly control parts of Bengal. S: Armenians establish a first settlement on the Malabar coast. T: Akbar allows Armenians to build a church in Agra. (a) Write the century of each event. (b) Arrange the five events from earliest to latest. (c) How many centuries separate the Armenians' first Malabar settlement from the Mughal period when they gained patronage? (d) Which event is about a community that was brought to India and did not come by choice?
questions.a: (a) Q: 7th century; S: 8th century; T: 16th century; P: mid-17th century; R: 18th century. (b) Q, S, T, P, R. (c) From the 8th to the 16th century, 8 centuries. (d) R: the Siddis were brought to India as slaves by Arab, Portuguese and British traders.
s: (a) Q 7th, S 8th, T 16th, P mid-17th, R 18th century
(b) Order Q, S, T, P, R
(c) 16 - 8 = 8 centuries
(d) R: the Siddis, brought as slaves

questions.q:
A heritage club in Surat is planning a trail called 'Traders who stayed'. Its notes from the chapter: Arab merchants came to India from the 7th century onward, settled along the west coast in Kerala, Gujarat and Karnataka, traded spices and other goods, married local women and formed new communities, becoming part of the Mappila Muslim community in Kerala. Armenian merchants traded in Indian spices and fine muslins; there is some evidence of a first settlement on the Malabar coast in the 8th century; in the 16th century Akbar let them build a church in Agra and follow their Christian practices; they served in the Mughal royal household, army and administration; in Kolkata the 18th-century Armenian College and Mother Mary Church continue to be active.
(a) Which kind of goods do the notes name for both communities?
(b) The trail has one stop on the Kerala (Malabar) coast, for the community with the earlier date. Using the earliest century the notes give for each community, which one is it, and by about how many centuries?
(c) The club also wants a stop where one community's institutions are still in use. Which city and which institutions should it choose?
(d) The club leader writes, 'Both communities gave up their own ways and simply merged into local communities.' Evaluate this with evidence for each community.
questions.a: (a) Spices. (b) The Arab merchants: 7th century, against the 8th century for the Armenians' first Malabar settlement, so about one century earlier (8 - 7 = 1). (c) Kolkata: the 18th-century Armenian College and Mother Mary Church continue to be active. (d) The claim is wrong. The Arab merchants did join local life (they married local women and became part of the Mappila Muslim community), but they also brought new ideas, culture and religion, so they did not simply give up their ways. The Armenians kept their own Christian faith (Akbar let them build a church and follow their practices, and their Kolkata church is still active) while serving in the Mughal household, army and administration; they became part of Indian life without merging into another community.
s: (a) Spices
(b) Arab merchants; 7th vs 8th century, about one century earlier
(c) Kolkata: Armenian College and Mother Mary Church still active
(d) Rejects the claim: Arabs joined the Mappilas but brought their own religion and ideas; Armenians kept their Christian faith while serving the Mughals

questions.q: The Lotus Temple in New Delhi is a house of worship of which community?
questions.a: The Lotus Temple in New Delhi is a Baha'i temple.

questions.q: The Baha'i religion began in Persia in the mid-1800s. Who led it?
questions.a: Baha'u'llah, whose teachings spoke of unity among all people and harmony between religions.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Some Baha'is left Iran and came to India from the late 19th century.
Reason (R): The ruling religious leadership in Iran branded them as heretics because of their different beliefs, and they were treated badly.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, and R explains A: branded heretics and treated badly in Iran, some Baha'is looked for safer places, and India was one of the first places they came to.

questions.q: (a) Name the Maharaja who rescued the Polish orphans, and the state he ruled (with its present-day name). (b) About how many orphans is he credited with saving, and between which years?
questions.a: (a) Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, the Maharaja of Nawanagar State (present-day Jamnagar). (b) Around a thousand Polish orphans, between 1942 and 1946.
s: (a) Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja of Nawanagar (Jamnagar)
(b) About a thousand orphans, 1942 to 1946

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) Between which years did the Second World War take place? (b) What happened to many children in Poland during that war? (c) In which city is the Good Maharaja Square, and whose service does its monument honour?
questions.a: (a) Between 1939 and 1945. (b) Poland was invaded, families were torn apart and many children were orphaned. (c) In Warsaw, Poland; it honours the Maharaja of Nawanagar, Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, for his help to the Polish people.
s: (b) Families torn apart; many children orphaned after the invasion
(c) Warsaw; honours the Maharaja of Nawanagar

questions.q: Which of these statements about the Maharaja of Nawanagar and the Polish children is NOT supported by the chapter?
o: The President of Poland honoured his service in 1946, as soon as the children had gone home.
He mobilised the Red Cross and other organisations to help him rescue the children.
He took the children to Jamnagar and gave them a safe place to stay, food and care.
He was touched by the tragedy of Polish families torn apart in the Second World War.
questions.a: The statement that Poland honoured him in 1946 is not supported: the chapter says his service was recognised by the President of Poland in the early 21st century, when the monument was built. The other three are in the chapter.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the 'Good Maharaja'.
I. Poland was invaded during the Second World War, which lasted from 1939 to 1945.
II. The Maharaja rescued the children on his own, without the help of any organisation.
III. His service was recognised by the President of Poland in the early 21st century, and a monument was built in his honour.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: he mobilised the Red Cross and other organisations to help him rescue the children.

questions.q: Two Indian rulers in this chapter took in people who had nowhere safe to go: Raja Jadi Rana of Sanjan and the Maharaja of Nawanagar. Compare them in four lines. (a) Whom did each take in, and why did those people need help? (b) What did each ruler give them? (c) How long did the guests stay in India? (d) Name one value from the chapter's section 'The Whole World is Family' that both rulers acted on, and give its meaning.
questions.a: (a) Jadi Rana took in the Parsis, who had fled religious persecution in Persia; the Maharaja took in Polish children orphaned when Poland was invaded in the Second World War (and several thousand other Polish refugees). (b) Jadi Rana gave the Parsis a secure place to settle in his kingdom; the Maharaja had the children rescued with the Red Cross and other organisations, brought them to Jamnagar, and gave them a safe place to stay, food and care. (c) The Parsis stayed for good and still live in India; the Polish children returned home safely after the war. (d) Atithi devo bhava, 'a guest is like God' (or vasudhaiva kutumbakam, 'the whole world is family').
s: (a) Parsis fleeing persecution in Persia; Polish war orphans
(b) A secure place to settle; rescue, a safe place, food and care in Jamnagar
(c) Parsis stayed for good; Polish children went home after the war
(d) Atithi devo bhava ('a guest is like God') or vasudhaiva kutumbakam, with its meaning

questions.q:
A Class 7 group in Mysuru is recording a radio talk called 'Faiths that found a home in India'. Their notes on one faith read: began in Persia (modern-day Iran) in the mid-1800s, led by Baha'u'llah; his teachings spoke of unity among all people and harmony between religions; the ruling religious leadership in Iran branded its followers heretics because of their different beliefs, and they were treated badly; some looked for safer places, and India was one of the first places they came to, from the late 19th century.
(a) Name the faith, and its house of worship in New Delhi shown in the chapter.
(b) A team member writes, 'They were persecuted in Iran because they were foreigners there.' Use the notes to show why this is wrong, and state the real reason.
(c) Using the chapter's meaning of 'heretic', explain why the leadership in Iran called them heretics.
(d) Apply the same meaning to the Syriac Christians. Does the heretic label explain all the persecution they faced, as it does for the Baha'is? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The Baha'i faith; the Lotus Temple in New Delhi. (b) The faith began in Persia itself, so its followers were not foreigners there; they were persecuted because the ruling religious leadership branded them heretics for their different beliefs. (c) A heretic is a person considered to hold beliefs, especially religious ones, contrary to the dominant view; the Baha'is held beliefs different from those of Iran's ruling religious leadership. (d) No. Under the Roman Empire the Syriac Christians were sometimes treated as heretics because some of their beliefs about Christ differed from those of the official Church, which fits the meaning; but in the Persian Empire they were persecuted because they were suspected of secretly helping the Romans, Persia's enemies, which is a political suspicion, not heresy. For the Baha'is the heretic label was the reason for their treatment.
s: (a) Baha'i faith; Lotus Temple, New Delhi
(b) It began in Persia, so not foreigners; branded heretics for different beliefs
(c) Heretic = beliefs contrary to the dominant view, applied to the Baha'is
(d) No: Rome called them heretics over beliefs about Christ, but Persia persecuted them on suspicion of helping the Romans

questions.q: The Parsis and the Baha'is both left Iran (Persia) for India, about a thousand years apart. Raghav says, 'The Baha'i story is simply the Parsi story repeated.' Compare the two communities under five heads, one line each: (1) when they began arriving in India; (2) who founded each faith, and whether it is old or new; (3) what each faith teaches, as the chapter gives it; (4) what in India today shows their faith; (5) who makes up the community in India today. End with your verdict on Raghav's claim.
questions.a: (1) Parsis: reached Gujarat between the 8th and 10th centuries; Baha'is: started arriving during the late 19th century. (2) Zoroastrianism was founded by the prophet Zarathushtra in Central Asia and is one of the world's oldest religions; the Baha'i faith is a new religion that began in Persia in the mid-1800s, led by Baha'u'llah. (3) Zoroastrianism: worship of one God, Ahura Mazda, and choosing good over evil; Baha'i: unity among all people and harmony between religions. (4) Parsis: the ancient sacred fire still burns at Udvada; Baha'is: the Lotus Temple in New Delhi is a Baha'i house of worship. (5) Parsis: the community that came and settled (India now has the largest Zoroastrian population in the world); Baha'is: most are Indians who joined the faith. Verdict: partly right at most. Both fled ill-treatment in the same land and found safety in India, but the faiths differ in age, founder and teaching, they came about a thousand years apart, and the Baha'i community in India today is mostly made up of Indians who joined it.
s: (1) Arrival: 8th-10th centuries vs late 19th century
(2) Zarathushtra, one of the oldest religions vs Baha'u'llah, a new faith of the mid-1800s
(3) One God Ahura Mazda, good over evil vs unity of all people, harmony between religions
(4) Sacred fire at Udvada vs Lotus Temple
(5) Settled community vs mostly Indians who joined, and a reasoned verdict

questions.q: Tibet, India's northern neighbour on the other side of the Himalayan range, is sometimes called by which name?
questions.a: The 'Land of Snows'.

questions.q: In which year did the 14th Dalai Lama flee across the Himalaya and receive asylum in India?
questions.a: In 1959, after a popular uprising in Lhasa against the Chinese presence.

questions.q:
Match each place in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Dharamshala  2. Bylakuppe  3. Lhasa  4. Nalanda
Column II: P. A centre of Buddhist learning destroyed in the 12th-13th centuries  Q. Seat of the Central Tibetan Administration  R. Site of a Tibetan monastery in Karnataka  S. Religious and administrative capital of Tibet in 1959
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Dharamshala is where the Central Tibetan Administration functions; Bylakuppe has a Tibetan monastery in Karnataka; Lhasa was Tibet's religious and administrative capital; Nalanda was destroyed in the 12th-13th centuries.

questions.q: True or False: Sowa Rigpa, the traditional medicine of the Tibetans, is also known as the 'Art of Healing'. Give the verdict and state when and where it was codified.
questions.a: True. Sowa Rigpa is also known as the 'Art of Healing'; it was codified in the 8th century CE by a medical council held near Lhasa in Tibet.
s: Verdict: True
Codified in the 8th century CE by a medical council near Lhasa

questions.q: State three things the Indian government did for the Tibetan refugees, as given in the chapter.
questions.a: (1) It rehabilitated the Tibetan refugees. (2) It provided education to their children. (3) It facilitated the creation of Tibetan settlements so that they could make India a second home and preserve their language, culture and heritage.
s: Rehabilitated the refugees
Provided education to their children
Facilitated Tibetan settlements to preserve language, culture and heritage

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Tibet became a centre of Buddhism in the 7th century.
Reason (R): After Nalanda was destroyed in the 12th and 13th centuries, many monks left for Tibet with Sanskrit manuscripts.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A: Tibet became a Buddhist centre in the 7th century because its king embraced the Buddha's teachings; the monks' journey after Nalanda's destruction came five or six centuries later.

questions.q: Tsering is listing the systems of medicine that the chapter says are supported by the Government of India's AYUSH programme. Which item should NOT be on her list?
questions.a: Acupuncture is not in the chapter's list. The chapter names Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa Rigpa and Homoeopathy.

questions.q: The chapter says the Central Tibetan Administration 'functions as a government-in-exile'. (a) From which Indian town does it function? (b) Explain why it is called a government 'in exile'.
questions.a: (a) Dharamshala, in Himachal Pradesh. (b) It works for the Tibetan people from outside their homeland, because China overran and annexed Tibet and the Dalai Lama had to flee to India in 1959.
s: (a) Dharamshala, Himachal Pradesh
(b) Works from outside Tibet because China annexed Tibet and its leader had to flee

questions.q:
Tenzin's family runs a stall in a Tibetan market in Goa, and his grandmother is treated with Tibetan medicine. For a board at the stall, Tenzin notes from the chapter: Sowa Rigpa, the 'Art of Healing', was codified in the 8th century CE by a medical council held near Lhasa; it blends ancient principles and practices of Ayurveda with inputs from China, Central Asia, Persia and even Greece; Tibetans began propagating it soon after taking refuge in India in 1959; Men-Tsee-Khang in Dharamshala practises it; it has been integrated into the Government of India's AYUSH programme.
(a) About how many years old was the codified system when Tibetans began propagating it in India? Show your working.
(b) Besides Ayurveda, name three places whose inputs went into Sowa Rigpa.
(c) For what two purposes does Men-Tsee-Khang use this system, according to the chapter?
(d) Tenzin must title the board either 'Sowa Rigpa: a gift India gave Tibet' or 'Sowa Rigpa: a system India and Tibet share'. Which title do the notes support better? Justify with two facts.
questions.a: (a) The 8th century CE runs from 701 to 800, so by 1959 the system was between 1959 - 800 = 1,159 and 1959 - 701 = 1,258 years old: about 1,200 years. (b) Any three of China, Central Asia, Persia and Greece. (c) To treat chronic diseases and to manage epidemics. (d) 'A system India and Tibet share'. It draws on Ayurveda but was codified in Tibet, near Lhasa, with inputs from China, Central Asia, Persia and Greece as well, so it was not simply India's gift; and today it is practised in India and is part of the Government of India's AYUSH programme, so both countries now hold it.
s: (b) Three of China, Central Asia, Persia, Greece
(c) Treating chronic diseases and managing epidemics
(d) 'Shared': codified in Tibet with many inputs besides Ayurveda, and now part of India's AYUSH

questions.q: One of the Dalai Lama's Four Commitments is 'the preservation of Tibetan culture'. Dolma says, 'Life in India has helped the Tibetans keep this commitment.' Evaluate her view with five separate pieces of evidence from the chapter, one line each, and end with your verdict.
questions.a: (1) The Indian government facilitated the creation of Tibetan settlements so that the community could preserve and promote its language, culture and heritage. (2) Many Tibetan monasteries patterned on the original ones in Tibet were established in India, particularly in Karnataka, so Tibetan Buddhists can pursue their way of life and spiritual practices without fear or hindrance. (3) Soon after taking refuge in 1959, Tibetans started propagating their traditional medicine, Sowa Rigpa, and institutions like Men-Tsee-Khang in Dharamshala practise it. (4) Sowa Rigpa has been integrated into the Government of India's AYUSH programme, so the tradition has official support. (5) The Dalai Lama lives in Dharamshala as an 'honoured guest', and the Central Tibetan Administration functions from there as a government-in-exile. Verdict: the view is well supported; India gave the Tibetans the settlements, monasteries and freedom they needed to keep their culture alive, while they also became part of Indian society.
s: Settlements to preserve and promote language, culture and heritage
Monasteries patterned on the originals, especially in Karnataka, without fear or hindrance
Sowa Rigpa propagated after 1959, practised at Men-Tsee-Khang
Sowa Rigpa integrated into AYUSH
Dalai Lama an 'honoured guest' in Dharamshala / Central Tibetan Administration, and a reasoned verdict

questions.q: Whose last message, quoted at the start of the chapter, says: 'No one is a stranger, my child; the whole world is your own'?
questions.a: Sri Sarada Devi, the spiritual consort of Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.

questions.q: The verse 'For the noble-minded, the whole world is family' opens the chapter. From which text is it taken?
questions.a: The Hitopadesha, from which the chapter quotes the line ending 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam'.

questions.q:
Match each phrase in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Vasudhaiva kutumbakam  2. Sarve bhavantu sukhinah  3. Atithi devo bhava  4. Karaniya Metta Sutta
Column II: P. May all creatures be happy  Q. The whole world is family  R. The Buddha's words on loving-kindness  S. A guest is like God
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means the whole world is family; sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all creatures be happy; atithi devo bhava, a guest is like God; the Karaniya Metta Sutta is the Buddha's words on loving-kindness.

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says it tells the story of every community that came to India from other parts of the world and settled here. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says there have been many such migrant communities in India's history, up to recent times, but it cannot cover them all and has selected only a few representative examples.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: it cannot cover them all and gives only a few representative examples

questions.q: The Karaniya Metta Sutta says that, 'even as a mother protects with her life her only child', one should cherish all living beings. (a) Whose words does the Sutta record, as its English title in the chapter shows? (b) Give one example of acting on this sentiment in school life.
questions.a: (a) The Buddha's: the chapter gives its title as 'The Buddha's Words on Loving-Kindness'. (b) Any suitable example of caring for every being, for example a student who looks after an injured stray puppy in the school ground as carefully as she would her own pet.
s: (a) The Buddha's
(b) A fitting school example of cherishing all beings

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas came intending to conquer India but were conquered instead by its culture.
Reason (R): Wherever there is a sizeable community of Indians living abroad today, it is perceived as peaceful and law-abiding.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A is about ancient invaders who came into India and were won over by its culture, philosophy, knowledge traditions, geography, climate and economy; R is about how Indians living in other countries are seen today.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements from the section 'The Whole World is Family'.
I. People made India their home either seeking refuge or seeing opportunities for prosperity and a good life.
II. India's many schools of thought, met in earlier chapters of 'Tapestry of the Past', taught ideas such as sarve bhavantu sukhinah and atithi devo bhava.
III. The Karaniya Metta Sutta expresses a sentiment opposite to these teachings.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: the chapter says the Karaniya Metta Sutta expresses the same sentiment beautifully.

questions.q: Neha says, 'According to the chapter, India became a haven for the persecuted mainly because of its geography.' Test her claim against the chapter in three points.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong. (1) The chapter says India developed a culture of peaceful coexistence and acceptance of diverse faiths, and that this innate character of its people and culture created a haven for the persecuted. (2) It traces this to the teachings of India's schools of thought, such as sarve bhavantu sukhinah, atithi devo bhava and the value of compassion. (3) On p. 141 geography appears only in the list of things (with culture, philosophy, knowledge traditions, climate and economy) that won over those who came to conquer, not as the reason India sheltered the persecuted.
s: Chapter credits a culture of peaceful coexistence and acceptance
Rooted in values such as sarve bhavantu sukhinah, atithi devo bhava, compassion
Geography appears only among the things that won over would-be conquerors, so the claim fails

questions.q:
For a wall timeline in a Bhopal school, the class copies one date for each group from the chapter, in the order in which the chapter tells the stories: Bene Israel, around 175 BCE (according to some scholars); Syriac Christians, difficulties from the 4th century CE; Parsis, reached Gujarat between the 8th and 10th centuries; Arab merchants, came from the 7th century onward; Baha'is, arrived from the late 19th century; Polish orphans, 1942-1946; Tibetans, 1959.
(a) Which two groups on the list came in the 20th century?
(b) One entry on the list gives the time when a group's troubles began, not when it reached India. Which group is it, and what does the chapter say about where it finally reached?
(c) Rahul says, 'The chapter tells the stories in exact time order.' Find the pair of groups on the list that breaks this order and explain.
(d) Using the earliest and latest years on the list, work out about how many years the list spans, and say whether 'centuries' or 'millennia' describes it better.
questions.a: (a) The Polish orphans (1942-1946) and the Tibetans (1959). (b) The Syriac Christians: the 4th century CE is when they began to face difficulties in West Asia; the chapter says some of them travelled eastward along trade routes and reached the Malabar coast (present-day Kerala), without giving a year of arrival. (c) The Parsis and the Arab merchants: the Parsis are told first but reached Gujarat between the 8th and 10th centuries, while the Arab merchants were already coming from the 7th century, so Rahul is wrong. (d) From 175 BCE to 1959 CE is 175 + 1959 - 1 = 2133 years (there is no year 0), a little over two thousand years, so 'millennia' fits better.
s: (a) Polish orphans and Tibetans
(b) Syriac Christians: 4th century is when troubles began; reached the Malabar coast, no arrival year given
(c) Parsis (8th-10th c.) told before Arab merchants (from the 7th c.), so not in exact order
(d) 175 + 1959 - 1 = 2133 years; 'millennia'

questions.q: The chapter's summary says India's values have 'enabled even small communities to find India a secure place and maintain here their traditions over centuries'. Test this claim with four communities: the Bene Israel, the Parsis, the Armenians and the Tibetans. For each, write one line giving (i) the date or period the chapter gives for its arrival, (ii) about how long it has been in India by 2026, and (iii) one tradition it has kept. In a fifth line, give your verdict on whether 'over centuries' fits all four.
questions.a: (1) Bene Israel: around 175 BCE (according to some scholars); over 2,000 years (175 + 2026 - 1 = 2,200); they kept their prayer that there is only one God. (2) Parsis: reached Gujarat between the 8th and 10th centuries; more than 1,000 years (2026 - 1000 = 1,026 at the least); their ancient sacred fire still burns at Udvada. (3) Armenians: Mughal-era settlements from the 16th century (with evidence of a Malabar settlement in the 8th century); more than 400 years (2026 - 1600 = 426 at the least); their Christian faith, with the Armenian College and Mother Mary Church in Kolkata still active. (4) Tibetans: 1959; 67 years (2026 - 1959); their Buddhist way of life in monasteries patterned on the originals, or Sowa Rigpa. Verdict: the claim fits the Bene Israel, the Parsis and the Armenians, who have kept their traditions over centuries; the Tibetans have kept theirs, but for decades, not yet centuries, so they show the same welcome at work more recently.
s: Bene Israel: around 175 BCE; over 2,000 years; prayer to one God
Parsis: 8th-10th centuries; over 1,000 years; sacred fire at Udvada
Armenians: 16th century; over 400 years; Christian faith / Kolkata church and college
Tibetans: 1959; 67 years; monasteries or Sowa Rigpa
Verdict: fits the first three; Tibetans kept traditions for decades, not centuries
